HARD FORMAT RULES (verify against the compiler; the compiler wins)
Files:
- `content/books/<slug>/book.yml`: `title`, `author`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `draft: false`.
- Chapter folders `NN-chapter-slug/` containing `chapter.yml` (`title`, `summary`, `draft: false`).
- Section files `NN-subchapter-slug.md` inside chapter folders. Names use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens only.
Front matter of every section: `title` and `questions` (5–7 questions).
Each question has: `id`, `prompt`, `type`, `explanation`, `options`.
- `id`: unique lowercase slug within the section (letters, digits, hyphens). NEVER `yes`, `no`, `true`, `false`, `null` (any case).
- `type`: ALWAYS present, either `single` (exactly 1 correct option) or `multiple` (2–3 correct options out of 5; the prompt must end with "Select all that apply.").
- `options`: 4–5 items; each has `text`; right answers also have `correct: true`; wrong answers have no `correct` key.
- `explanation`: required on every question and fully self-contained. Structure: (a) the exact hardware or OS mechanism that makes the correct option(s) true; (b) why EACH distractor fails, naming the specific misconception; (c) all latency, alignment, padding, or cache-line arithmetic step by step. Refer to options by their text, NEVER by letter or position (e.g., never "option B").
YAML safety:
- Double-quote every string value (`title`, `id`, `prompt`, option `text`, `summary`, etc.). Escape inner double quotes. This avoids boolean/number/null coercion and `: ` / ` #` / leading `` ` `` `@` `[` `{` `*` `- ` problems (e.g., option text `"64"`, `"4096"`, `"No"`).
- Long explanations: use a block scalar (`explanation: |-` with indented lines) if the compiler or existing books accept it; otherwise a double-quoted string. Test with the real compiler on the first section before writing the rest.
- Never put `---` at the start of a line inside front matter content.
Markdown body:
- The body starts with `## Learning objectives` (3–5 bullets), then the structure below.
- Every fenced code block has a language tag from this set, intersected with what `SyntaxHighlighter` supports: `csharp`, `python`, `javascript`, `sql`, `bash`, `json`, `yaml`, `html`. Use `csharp` for struct layouts, padding, atomics, and memory-ordering examples (with comments), and `bash` for `perf`, `strace`, `lscpu`, and similar commands. Use Markdown tables for latency hierarchies, cache geometry, and memory layouts. Keep snippets short and exact.
Answer-position balance (the UI does not shuffle): for question number k (1-based) in section number s of the book, place the first correct option at index ((k + s) mod n), 0-based, where n is that question's option count; for `multiple` questions, place correct options at that index and the next valid index(es). validate.py must verify that no position holds more than 40% of the correct answers within any section.

SECTION STRUCTURE (400–1200 words of prose per section, one crisp concept each)
1. `## Learning objectives`
2. `## The invariant` : the timeless mechanism, stated precisely, with the primary-source or architecture-manual basis.
3. `## Worked example` : concrete numbers, a layout or access-pattern trace, or a short code sample with exact expected behavior.
4. `## Where this shows up today` : the relevance block (see policy below).
5. `## Pitfalls checklist` : 3–6 bullets of mistakes engineers actually make.
6. `## Key takeaways` : 3–5 bullets.

TIMELESS-VS-CURRENT POLICY (apply strictly)
- At most ONE question per section may depend on a fact that could change within five years (specific cache sizes, page-size defaults, hardware generations). All other questions must rest on invariants: how caches, paging, coherence, atomics, and I/O stacks work and the arithmetic that follows.
- Numeric hardware figures (latencies, sizes) are order-of-magnitude and must be labeled "typical" with a rough range; questions may rely on them only as ratios or orders of magnitude, or when the question itself states the numbers.
- The "Where this shows up today" block is at most about 15% of the section. It connects the invariant to how the world looks in 2026: current CPUs, kernels, runtimes, cloud hardware. Every dated claim must be written as "As of November 2026, ..." and, if it names a CPU family, OS, runtime, or version, include it. Name products only as examples of a mechanism, never as the point.
- If web access is available, verify every dated claim against primary sources (architecture manuals, kernel documentation, man-pages, vendor docs, runtime release notes) before writing it. If you cannot verify a current-state claim, drop it or restate it as a general mechanism. Never guess specs.
- Citations: cite sources at document level (Drepper; Arpaci-Dusseau OSTEP; Hennessy and Patterson; Intel, AMD, and Arm architecture manuals; Linux man-pages such as `mmap(2)`, `fsync(2)`, `epoll(7)`, `io_uring(7)`; the C++ and .NET memory-model specifications; Lamport 1979 for sequential consistency); add chapter or section numbers only when confirmed. Never fabricate a quote or number. Always separate architecture-independent invariants from x86-64 or Arm64 specifics, and OS-independent concepts from Linux, Windows, or macOS specifics.
- Dated facts must never be the only reason an answer is correct.

QUESTION QUALITY RULES
- Mix per section: at least 2 compute-or-trace questions, at least 1 "spot the bug / why is this slow" question, and the rest conceptual or scenario-based.
- Distractors are real misconceptions, plausible and parallel in length and style; the correct option must not be systematically the longest.
- No "all of the above" or "none of the above". No trick wording. No negations in stems unless emphasized with NOT.
- Every question must be answerable using only what that section teaches plus the explanation. No concept is tested twice across the whole book except in Chapter 7 (review), which must combine concepts from earlier chapters.
- Prompts are Markdown; use inline code for identifiers and values. State assumptions (e.g., "64-byte cache lines, 4 KB pages") inside the prompt whenever the answer depends on them.

EXEMPLAR (shape only; do not copy its content)
````markdown
---
title: "Integer Division Truncation"
questions:
  - id: "negative-division"
    type: "single"
    prompt: "In C#, what does `-7 / 2` evaluate to?"
    explanation: |-
      C# integer division truncates toward zero, so the exact quotient -3.5 becomes -3.
      "-4" is what floor division would give (as in Python's `//`), but C# does not floor.
      "-3.5" is wrong because both operands are `int`, so the result is `int`.
      "4" ignores the sign entirely.
      Arithmetic: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1, so |quotient| = 3; the sign is negative, giving -3.
    options:
      - text: "-4"
      - text: "-3"
        correct: true
      - text: "-3.5"
      - text: "4"
---

## Learning objectives

- Predict the result of integer division for negative operands.

## The invariant

...
````

BOOK SPECIFICATION
- Slug: cpu-memory-and-os
- Title: "CPU, Memory & OS Mechanical Sympathy"
- Summary: "The hardware and operating-system invariants that govern real program performance: CPU caches, virtual memory, atomics and memory ordering, syscalls, and storage durability."
- Tags: [systems, performance, cpu, memory, concurrency, operating-systems]
- Author/date: author id per Step 0; `date` = 2026-11-27 in the repo's date format.
- Audience: working software engineers (often in managed languages such as C#, Java, Python, JavaScript) who want to understand why code is fast or slow. Prerequisites: basic programming, binary and hexadecimal. Examples use C#-like or clear pseudocode in `csharp` blocks.

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-latency-scales-and-cpu-pipeline-realities: the order-of-magnitude latency hierarchy (cycle, L1, L2, L3, DRAM, NVMe, same-datacenter network, cross-region), instruction pipelining, superscalar execution, out-of-order execution, branch prediction and the cost of mispredictions, branchless vs predictable code, SIMD data-level parallelism. Today: heterogeneous performance and efficiency cores, and how speculative-execution vulnerabilities (Spectre class) changed OS and runtime costs (mechanism-level; verify specifics).
02-cpu-caches-and-memory-layout: cache lines (typically 64 bytes), spatial vs temporal locality, pointer chasing vs contiguous arrays, array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays with byte-level math, strided access and hardware prefetching, set associativity and conflict misses (power-of-two strides), working-set size vs cache size, NUMA and remote-memory penalties. Today: large stacked or shared last-level caches, chiplet topologies and their effect on core-to-core latency (verify before naming products or sizes).
03-cache-coherence-false-sharing-and-alignment: MESI/MOESI intuition, cache-line ping-pong, false sharing between independent variables on one line, field alignment and padding arithmetic, struct layout rules, padding counters and ring-buffer indexes to separate lines, `[StructLayout]`/`[FieldOffset]`/`[Padding]-style` techniques in .NET at the concept level. Today: how to detect false sharing with hardware performance counters and profilers (verify tool names and options).
04-virtual-memory-pages-and-processes: virtual vs physical address spaces, multi-level page tables and walk cost, page sizes (4 KB, 2 MB, 1 GB; note Arm platforms with other base page sizes), TLB reach and misses, shootdowns, minor vs major page faults, `mmap`, copy-on-write and `fork`, overcommit and the OOM killer concept, stack vs heap cost, direct and indirect context-switch costs. Today: transparent huge pages trade-offs, memory-mapped files in databases and runtimes, containers and cgroup memory limits (verify details).
05-synchronization-atomics-and-memory-models: race conditions vs data races, mutexes (futex-style fast paths) vs spinlocks vs hybrid locks, lock convoys, priority inversion, atomic read-modify-write and compare-and-swap, the ABA problem, store buffers and reordering, sequential consistency vs acquire-release vs relaxed ordering, `volatile` misconceptions, lock-free is not wait-free. Today: why weakly ordered architectures (Arm64) expose bugs that x86-64 hides; language memory models in C++, Java, .NET, Rust (verify claims against specifications).
06-system-calls-io-models-and-storage-durability: user/kernel mode switches, system-call cost and the vDSO, blocking vs non-blocking I/O, `select`/`poll` O(N) scanning vs `epoll`/`kqueue` readiness vs `io_uring`/IOCP completion models, the page cache and write-back, exactly what `write`, `fflush`, `fsync`, `fdatasync`, and directory `fsync` guarantee, crash-safe atomic replacement (write temp, fsync file, rename, fsync directory), `O_DIRECT`, torn writes, device write caches and power-loss protection. Today: NVMe latency changing the balance between CPU and storage, `io_uring` adoption and its security posture, cloud block-storage durability semantics (verify against docs).
07-cross-chapter-review-and-performance-diagnosis: diagnosing bottlenecks from profiler or counter symptoms (high IPC vs memory-bound stalls, high system-CPU time, lock contention vs false sharing, TLB-miss-heavy workloads, silent durability loss after power cut). Each question presents a short realistic symptom set and asks for the most likely mechanism and the right first measurement or fix.
